new_statements.quote: Stress, in this grammar, is defined as loudness. The default stress falls on the last syllable. ili [ɛˈli] 'go.IRR.NFUT', tobo̊u [tʌˈβo] 'speak', ... sibigi [siβiˈgi] 'dirt', sisigo [sĩsĩˈgɔ̃] 'children', moso=ko̊u [mɔ̃sɔ̃ˈko] 'house=LOC'. However, even though stress is mostly predictable, and therefore non-phonemic, it may vary on the same word in isolation. ... kafei [ˈkaɸeɪ] or [kaˈɸeɪ] 'blood', sosi [ˈsɔsi] or [sɔˈsi] 'ant'. In fact, the data we have is inconsistent. Working with one man using the Speech Analyzer, the default stress in his speech is indeed on the final syllable. Still, in about 9% of the words we have analysed, we can only partly explain why the stress is not on the final syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (Årsjö 2016, 336 pp., SIL PNG; downloaded via Internet Archive copy of sil.org REAP, listed). extracted text locates 'default stress falls' on PDF page 28 (= printed p. 28); I rendered pp. 28-29 at 130 dpi and read them. Printed p. 28, sec. 2.6.3 'Stress', reads exactly: 'Stress, in this grammar, is defined as loudness. The default stress falls on the last syllable.' followed by the example table ili [ɛˈl̪i] 'go.IRR.NFUT', toboů [t̪ʌˈβo] 'speak', temе̱ [t̪ʌ̃ˈmæ̃], sese̱ [sɛ̃ˈsæ̃], giyoů [gi.ˈo], miye̱ [mĩ.ˈæ̃], kueya [kʷɛɪˈɑ], sibigi [siβiˈgi], sisigo̱ [sĩsĩˈgɔ̃], moso̱=koů [mɔ̃sɒ̃ˈko] 'house=LOC' -- all with the stress mark before the final syllable; then 'However, even thou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (measured instrumentally as amplitude/loudness) is non-contrastive and by default falls on the word-final syllable, including on stress-bearing enclitics (moso=ko 'house=LOC' stressed on the clitic); about 9% of ~300 instrumentally analysed words deviate. Konai additionally has phonemic word-level tone (fall-rise, rising, rise-fall, falling, fall-fall patterns) independent of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; CaCi words may show 'equal stress' on both syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) some enclitics do not take stress (=ha² 'genitive/control', =me 'topic marker'), so stress stays on the host's final syllable; (ii) loan words (ikoke 'nail', subulu 'sweet potato', meleki 'dish') with non-final stress; (iii) words of shape CaCi often have equal stress or initial stress (gali, habi, sabi); (iv) 'bleed-through' words (mulo, bigile) that sound penultimate-stressed but are instrumentally final-stressed; stress on a given word may vary across repetitions in isolation.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word including stress-bearing enclitics; based on ~300 words recorded mostly in isolation from one main speaker (Speech Analyzer) plus earlier CECIL recordings; author notes isolation testing is unreliable and utterance-final syllables are lengthened regardless of stress. Language also has phonemic word tone (sec. 2.6.2), so this is a tonal language with an explicit stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Årsjö descriptions cover Konai (kxw, kona1242) as a whole; data from all villages except Tougohai, main instrumental speaker from Sesenabi/Dahamo (Lowland/Foothill/Mountain dialects said to share the same phonology). The two Fembe-like villages (Oguotibi, Tougohai) are excluded. No dialect-level glottocode distinction needed.

sources.note: Sec. 2.6.3 Stress (p. 28-29): stress defined as loudness; 'The default stress falls on the last syllable'; mostly predictable hence non-phonemic; ~9% of ~300 instrumentally analysed words non-final, attributed to unstressed enclitics (=ha genitive, =me topic), loan words, CaCi words (equal stress or initial), and 'bleed-through'. Separate phonemic word tone (2.6.2) and phonemic word nasalisation; length non-phonemic, stressed syllables longer.
